p.title: Shadowing and shielding: Effective heuristics for continuous influence maximisation in the voting dynamics

ext.title: Shadowing and shielding: Effective heuristics for continuous influence maximisation in the voting dynamics
ext.venue: PLOS ONE 16(6): e0252515 (published June 18, 2021; received Jan 26, 2021; accepted May 17, 2021). Metadata hint confirmed.
ext.document_type: Research article: analytical (heterogeneous mean-field) plus numerical simulation (gradient ascent, stochastic hill-climbing) on a single empirical network. No empirical election or lobbying data.
ext.coverage: Read the full extracted text file (1366 lines; 80,840 chars, slightly more than the 80,401 in the task hint) in four chunks: front matter, abstract, introduction, model, results, discussion, methods, heuristics, Table 1, supporting-information note, and the full reference list (refs 1-62). Page locations are inferred from the PLOS page-footer markers ("N / 21"). Not in the text file: the S1 Appendix (cited for other topologies, Figs 2-3, 5-14, Sections 1-12) and the figures themselves, so statements about those are unverified. Paul's markup: no annotation files were read, per the task's "(none)" instruction, so paul_markup is empty.
ext.research_question: How do optimal influence allocations differ between the continuous regime (flexible intensity per node) and the discrete regime (K nodes at fixed gain) in influence maximisation for the voter model with zealots? Can three heuristics (hub/degree preference, shadowing, shielding) explain optimal allocations? How exploitable is a passive opponent, and what is the pure-strategy Nash equilibrium when two active controllers optimise simultaneously? (Abstract p.1; Introduction pp.2-3.)
ext.theory: Voter model with external controllers (zealots) on a weighted network. Each node's probability of holding opinion A follows a rate equation (Eq 1, p.3). Steady state solves (L + Wa + Wb)x = wa (p.3); vote share X is Eq 2 (p.4). Controller A is active, controller B passive, both with budgets (Eq 3, p.4). Theoretical lenses: "shadowing" (first-order, target the opponent's nodes), "shielding" (second-order, target neighbours of the opponent's nodes), and degree preference (hub targeting). Analytical solution via a heterogeneous mean-field (HMF) approximation (Eq 4, p.5; Eqs 10-12, p.14) with series expansions in the low-allocation (w << d) and high-allocation (w >> d) limits (pp.6-8). Proof of concavity and uniqueness of the Nash equilibrium is deferred to S1 Appendix Section 12.
ext.data: Single empirical network: email interchange network of members of the Universitat Rovira i Virgili (Tarragona), N = 1133 nodes, taken from Guimerà et al. 2003 (ref 49; S1 Dataset). Unit of analysis: individual node (agent). Time period: not stated in the article. Edge count: not stated in the text. Synthetic/other topologies are referenced only to S1 Appendix Section 11 and Figs 10, 12, 13, which are not in the text file. Budget convention: B_a + B_b = N<d>/30 in most experiments; Fig 1 uses B = N<d>/60 per controller. Passive opponent typically targets K = 16 random nodes (discrete); K values up to 256 are used in Fig 3 and K varies in Fig 1b-c.
ext.method: Numerical optimisation for the active controller. Continuous: gradient ascent with step size mu = 50 and tolerance 1e-10, projection onto the N-simplex, backtracking, O(N^3/epsilon) cost (Methods, pp.15-16). Discrete: stochastic hill-climbing for 20N iterations or until no change in the last 10N (p.16). Analytical: HMF approximation and series expansions in the low and high allocation limits (Eqs 5-8, pp.7-8). Game-theoretic: iterated elimination of dominated strategies with gradient ascent to find the pure-strategy Nash equilibrium (p.13). Heuristics compared by vote-share gap ΔX against the numerical optimum, with binary-search tuning of heuristic parameters (pp.16-17, Table 1). Reported results are averages over 15 instances (K=16, Fig 6) or 15 and 60 instances elsewhere (Fig 4, Fig 5).
ext.identification: Not applicable in the econometric sense. No causal or statistical identification strategy. The "explanatory" claim rests on (a) visual and group-overlap analysis of numerical optima (Figs 1, 3, 4), (b) rank correlations between allocation and degree (Fig 5), and (c) comparing vote-share gaps of heuristics to the numerical optimum (Fig 6).
ext.scope: Population: one 1133-node email network (URV Tarragona), treated as a typical social-network topology; the paper claims results generalise to complex networks (S1 Appendix, not checked here). Institution: none; the network is an academic email network, not a political population. Era: not stated; the reference data is from 2003. Political relevance is framed only in general terms ("political competition", "winner-takes-all scenarios such as political elections or referendums", p.6). The model is abstract opinion dynamics, not calibrated to any election or lobbying outcome.

key_findings.finding: Optimal continuous allocations are spread widely across the network rather than concentrated on a few hubs. Around 111 of 1133 nodes (|H|+|A|, about 10%) get above-average allocation; 1013 nodes (V) are mostly flat (std/mean = 0.11); 9 nodes get zero (text also says 7 at p.5). Allocations range from 0.1 to 5.
key_findings.location: Results, 'Structure of optimal allocations in the continuous regime', p.5, lines 285-308, Fig 1a (K=16, equal budgets)
key_findings.numbers: |H|+|A| = 111; |V| = 1013; |Z| = 9 (and 7 at line 307); std/mean = 0.11; alloc range 1e-1 to 5

key_findings.finding: Entropy of the continuous optimal allocation distribution is considerably higher than for discrete allocations, across K and budget ratios. The gap widens as the passive controller spreads over more nodes.
key_findings.location: Results p.5-6, Fig 1b, lines 310-336 (entropy normalised by log N)
key_findings.numbers: No numeric values in text; qualitative only

key_findings.finding: Continuous allocation improves vote share over the best discrete allocation. Gain is about 5-10% for passive K < 100 and falls below 5% for K > 100.
key_findings.location: Results p.6, Fig 1c, lines 337-345; measure (X_cont - X_disc)/X_disc
key_findings.numbers: Relative improvement 5-10% for K < 100; < 5% for K > 100

key_findings.finding: Discrete optima are driven mainly by node degree (hub targeting); in the continuous regime shadowing plus shielding is the main explanatory factor, with degree effects weaker across scenarios.
key_findings.location: Results p.12, lines 737-755; Discussion p.13, lines 792-795

key_findings.finding: Shielding explains the group structure of continuous optima: very high (H) and zero (Z) allocations fall mainly on the opponent's targets (Tb); above-average (A) on their neighbours (Nb); below-average (V) on the rest (R).
key_findings.location: Results p.10, lines 607-613, Fig 4a (K=16); Fig 4 caption p.9
key_findings.numbers: Qualitative overlap; no percentages in text

key_findings.finding: Shielding is second-order and weakens as K grows. With budget disadvantage, anti-shielding (avoiding neighbours of opponent targets) also appears.
key_findings.numbers: Shielding weaker at K = 256 (Fig 3c); Nb below R for K > 5 under budget disadvantage

key_findings.finding: Degree correlation of optimal allocations is a by-product of shielding. Kendall tau between allocation and degree is above 0.5 for K > 30 in both optimal and pure-shielding strategies, but below |0.25| for optimal allocations when the passive controller targets low-degree-neighbour nodes. Shielding then gives tau down to about -0.5.
key_findings.numbers: tau > 0.5 for K > 30 (Fig 5b); |tau| < 0.25 for optimal in Fig 5c; shielding tau down to ~ -0.5

key_findings.finding: Heuristic vote-share gaps relative to the numerical optimum (K=16 passive, discrete). Budget advantage: continuous shadowing+shielding best at 1.89e-3 (shadowing alone 2.55e-3; discrete shadowing 1.58e-2; discrete degree 2.41e-2). Budget equality: discrete degree 8.99e-3 closest; continuous shadowing+shielding 2.97e-3; other continuous heuristics 5.5e-3 to 7.0e-3. Budget disadvantage: discrete degree 2.12e-3; continuous shadowing+shielding 7.28e-4; other continuous 2.33e-3 to 4.44e-3.
key_findings.numbers: Advantage: cont shadw+shield 1.89e-3, shadw 2.55e-3, unif 2.14e-2, deg 2.09e-2; Equality: cont shadw+shield 2.97e-3, discrete deg 8.99e-3; Disadvantage: cont shadw+shield 7.28e-4, discrete deg 2.12e-3

key_findings.finding: Analytical low-allocation limit (w << d): optimal w_ai is linear in opponent allocation w_bi and degree d_i with coefficient (Ba/Bb - 1). Positive coefficient (Ba > Bb) gives shadowing; negative (Ba < Bb) gives avoidance. Degree dependence only enters when positivity constraints bind, and then it favours low-degree nodes.

Vote share in the low limit is X_L = Ba/(Ba+Bb) + Bb/(4N^2) * sum_i (1 - w_bi/<w_b>)^2 / d_i, with <w_b> = Bb/N. A passive controller is more exploitable the more her allocation deviates from uniform, and the penalty is larger on low-degree nodes.

High limit (w >> d): optimal allocation depends on opponent allocation non-linearly and on budget, with no degree dependence. Vote share X_H = 1 - (Bb/(Ba+Bb)) * (1/N) sum_i (sqrt(w_bi/<w_b>) - 1)^2 (sic; as printed). Exploitability is independent of which nodes are misallocated.

Two active controllers: the unique pure-strategy Nash equilibrium is that both controllers target all nodes equally, w_ai = Ba/N and w_bi = Bb/N, regardless of network type and budgets. Numerically, normalised std of allocations converges to zero (S1 Appendix Fig 7).
key_findings.location: Results p.13, lines 758-782; Abstract p.1 lines 20-22
key_findings.numbers: w_ai = Ba/N; w_bi = Bb/N; normalised std -> 0

key_findings.finding: Gradient ascent is guaranteed to reach an epsilon-approximate solution in O(1/epsilon) iterations. Each step needs an N x N inversion, so cost is O(N^3/epsilon). Experiments used mu = 50, epsilon = 1e-10; all runs converged within 1e5 iterations.

measures: Steady-state vote share X (fraction of nodes holding opinion A, Eq 2)
Normalised entropy of allocation distribution H(w_a) = -log(N) sum_i (w_ai/Ba) log(w_ai/Ba)
Vote-share gap ΔX of each heuristic relative to numerical optimum
Allocation groups H, A, V, Z (high, above-average, below-average, zero) relative to mean allocation <w_a>
Shielding groups Tb (opponent targets), Nb (neighbours of opponent targets), R (rest)
Kendall rank correlation tau between allocation w_ai and degree d_i
Conditional probabilities P(i in A | d_i) and P(i in Nb | d_i)
Normalised standard deviation of allocations (std/mean), used as convergence test for Nash equilibrium
limitations: Strategies are time-invariant; campaigns that vary allocation over time are not modelled (p.14, lines 849-852; extensions cited to refs 54, 57).

Only one empirical network (URV email, N = 1133), described as well-mixed, without strong communities, and with little degree assortativity (p.14, lines 846-848). Generalisation to other topologies rests on S1 Appendix, which is not in the text file.
Only the voter model is studied. Ising and SIR extensions are proposed but not done (p.14, lines 844-846).
No noise in opinion dynamics. The authors note degree dependence might arise with noise, citing Lynn & Lee (p.14, lines 833-841).
The main analysis assumes a passive opponent. Two-active-controller results are limited to the uniform Nash equilibrium (p.13).

The HMF approximation is not always valid, ignores higher-order correlations, and is only reasonable for not overly sparse networks (p.15, lines 886-889). Analytical expressions rest on series expansions in the low and high allocation limits (p.7, lines 409-413).
Discrete optima come from stochastic hill-climbing, which only guarantees a global optimum for convex problems (p.16, lines 993-995). Discrete comparisons may therefore be sub-optimal.
Internal inconsistency: the count of zero-allocation nodes is |Z| = 9 at p.5 line 302 and |Z| = 7 at line 307 on the same page.
Political application is framed only qualitatively (winner-takes-all elections, p.6). No empirical election, lobbying or campaign data is used.
Heuristics need network structure, opponent strategy, or parameter tuning that a real campaigner may lack (Table 1, p.17).
references_of_note: Brede M, Restocchi V, Stein S (2018) Resisting Influence: How the Strength of Predispositions to Resist Control Can Change Strategies for Optimal Opinion Control in the Voter Model. Front. Robot. AI 5:34 (ref 26). Shows hub preference can shift to periphery when resistance is present; the discrete-regime benchmark this paper builds on.

Masuda N (2015) Opinion control in complex networks. New J. Phys. 17:033031 (ref 33). Zealot placement and controller-based opinion control in the voter model; the discrete influence-maximisation benchmark.

Romero Moreno G, Tran-Thanh L, Brede M (2020) Shielding and Shadowing: A Tale of Two Strategies for Opinion Control in the Voting Dynamics. Complex Networks VIII (ref 43). The earlier paper that introduced shadowing and shielding; this article extends it to general networks and the continuous regime.

Romero Moreno G, Tran-Thanh L, Brede M (2020) Continuous Influence Maximisation for the Voter Dynamics: Is Targeting High-Degree Nodes a Good Strategy? AAMAS 2020 (ref 44). Continuous-regime precursor on the degree-preference question.
Kempe D, Kleinberg J, Tardos E (2003) Maximizing the Spread of Influence Through a Social Network. KDD (ref 11). Canonical discrete influence-maximisation framing with budget constraints.

Chakraborty S, Stein S, Brede M, Swami A, de Mel G, Restocchi V (2019) Competitive influence maximisation using voting dynamics. ASONAM (ref 47). Competitive IM in the voter model; the author group's earlier work.

Brede M, Restocchi V, Stein S (2019) Transmission errors and influence maximization in the voter model. J. Stat. Mech. (ref 48). Noise in influence maximisation; relevant to the noise extension the paper proposes.

Brede M, Restocchi V, Stein S (2019) Effects of time horizons on influence maximization in the voter dynamics. J. Complex Networks (ref 54). Time-horizon dependence; the paper's dynamic-allocation caveat points here.

Lynn CW, Lee DD (2017) Statistical mechanics of influence maximization with thermal noise. EPL (ref 25). Continuous IM under Ising noise with degree dependence, contrasted with this paper's no-degree result.
Eshghi S et al. (2020) Spread, Then Target, and Advertise in Waves: Optimal Budget Allocation Across Advertising Channels. IEEE TNSE (ref 42). Continuous budget allocation in an applied setting.

Braha D, de Aguiar MAM (2017) Voting contagion: Modeling and analysis of a century of U.S. presidential elections. PLOS ONE (ref 30). Voter-model fit to real election data; the nearest election-data link in the reference list.
Guimerà R et al. (2003) Self-similar community structure in a network of human interactions. Phys. Rev. E (ref 49). Source of the URV email network used as the only empirical topology.

short_quotes.quote: Optimal allocations can be explained almost perfectly by the shielding heuristics without the need for additional assumptions about degree preference.
short_quotes.location: Results, 'Hub preferences and dependence on node degree', p.11, lines 680-681

short_quotes.quote: their explanatory power is strongly reduced in the continuous regime.
the unique pure Nash equilibrium is to target all nodes equally.

rel.summary_md:
Romero Moreno, Chakraborty and Brede (PLOS ONE 2021) study influence maximisation in a voter model with zealots. An active controller spreads a budget over the nodes of one 1,133-node university email network against a passive opponent whose allocation is fixed and known. They compare a discrete regime (K nodes at fixed gain) with a continuous regime (any intensity per node). The continuous optimum is spread out: about 111 of 1,133 nodes get above-average allocation, and the remaining mass is near uniform (std/mean 0.11). It beats the best discrete plan by 5-10% when the opponent targets fewer than 100 nodes.

Hub (degree) targeting explains discrete optima but explains little in the continuous regime. Two heuristics do: shadowing (spend where the opponent spends) and shielding (spend on the neighbours of the opponent's targets). Continuous shadowing plus shielding comes within 1.89e-3 of optimal vote share under budget advantage, against 2.09e-2 for degree targeting. In the low-allocation limit the best response is linear in the opponent's spend, with coefficient (Ba/Bb − 1): a richer controller shadows the opponent and a poorer one avoids the opponent's nodes. When both controllers optimise, the unique pure Nash equilibrium is uniform allocation. The paper uses no political data, no lobbying data and no noise.

The paper matters here because Melange's money layer is exactly this setup. optimize.py allocates a CU pot in $500 steps against fixed industry money, a passive opponent, and pflip is a single-node a/(a+b) vote-share form. In the system, though, money acts only on the funded member's own pflip and never spreads to neighbours, so shielding cannot emerge. An opponent-share field w_b already exists, labelled for a "shadowing layer", but no engine reads it. The contested-bills registry cites this paper for a counterparty term that no code uses yet. The paper's support is theoretical and comes from one network, so it supports the design concept and gives no calibration.

bearings.paper_claim: Against a passive opponent with known allocation w_b, the low-allocation optimum is w_ai linear in w_bi with coefficient c = (Ba/Bb − 1): shadow if Ba > Bb, avoid if Ba < Bb (Eq 5). Continuous shadowing+shielding comes within 1.89e-3 of the numerical optimum under budget advantage, against 2.09e-2 for degree targeting and 2.14e-2 for uniform. Under disadvantage it comes within 7.28e-4, against 2.12e-3 for discrete degree targeting (K=16, Fig 6).
bearings.system_side: The registry gives contested bills a per-bill counterparty set, but its docstring says 'no consumer exists today' (CONTESTED_V1 is a future dial). Separately, build_opposition_prior.py builds a per-member opposition share w_b that sums to 1.0, with consumer listed as 'coalition-builder adversary substrate / shadowing layer'. No engine file imports it (VERIFIED by searching fec/engine, moneyball_core.py and the templates for opposition_prior).
bearings.transfer_conditions: Carries over only as a design template: (1) the opponent's allocation is observed per member, which w_b approximates from FEC opposition money and not from LDA (D-021); (2) the opponent is passive within the planning horizon. The paper's dynamics are an unnoised voter model on an academic email network, so the coefficient (Ba/Bb − 1) and the gap sizes are not calibrated for Congress. Which side holds the budget advantage must be measured per bill before the sign of the response is chosen. UNVERIFIED for this system until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: With a passive opponent, the continuous optimum spreads widely: |H|+|A| = 111 of 1,133 nodes above average, |V| = 1,013 near-flat (std/mean 0.11). It beats the best discrete plan by 5-10% for opponent K < 100. When two active controllers optimise simultaneously, the unique pure Nash equilibrium is uniform allocation (w_ai = Ba/N), whatever the network or budgets.
bearings.paper_location: Results p.5 Fig 1a (lines 285-308); p.6 Fig 1c (lines 337-345); p.13 (lines 758-782)
bearings.system_side: CELF lazy greedy spends a $2.5M pot in $500 chunks with a $10k per-member cap. Industry money ind is fixed at fm.ind0 throughout, so industry is a passive opponent. The marginal of a chunk on member m changes only m's own pflip (marg_at sums tgt[m]·Δpflip over topics). CU dollars do not change neighbours' nA/nB, which are set by stance camps.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's spread and shielding results come from money propagating through the network's steady state. Melange's money term is node-local, so neither can arise in this optimizer; only shadowing-like behaviour through the b term of a/(a+b) can. The Nash result means the plan is a best response to a frozen opponent and could be exploited if industry PACs re-optimise. The paper's game is an idealised voter-model game, so this is a qualitative caution only. Equal-budget and per-candidate FEC limits have no analogue in the paper.

bearings.paper_claim: Steady-state opinion of node i in the voter model with zealots solves (L + Wa + Wb)x = wa. Each node's A-share is a ratio of A-pull (neighbours' state plus wa_i) to total pull (d_i + wa_i + wb_i) (Eq 1-2). In the high-allocation limit (w >> d) the optimum has no degree dependence (Eqs 7-8).
bearings.paper_location: Model p.3 Eq 1-2; Results pp.7-8 Eqs 7-8 (lines 487-539)
bearings.system_side: pflip = a/(a+b), where a = WM·pm·saturating CU money + WP·nA/mAt and b mirrors it with industry money and anti neighbours. Neighbour pull comes from stance-labelled camps normalised by the network maximum. It is a one-shot ratio, not a self-consistent steady state.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The functional form is analogous: both are share-of-pull ratios. The paper's analytics need neighbour states to be endogenous; Melange fixes them from category_stance.json, so the paper's HMF results do not apply directly. The analogy supports reading pflip as a voter-model-style vote-share proxy, never as a vote or access probability (D-025).

bearings.paper_claim: The degree correlation of optimal allocations is a by-product of shielding: Kendall tau > 0.5 for K > 30 for both optimal and pure-shielding plans. When the opponent targets nodes with low-degree neighbours, |tau| for the optimum falls below 0.25 and shielding gives tau down to about −0.5 (Fig 5b-c). 'Optimal allocations can be explained almost perfectly by the shielding heuristics without the need for additional assumptions about degree preference' (p.11).
bearings.system_side: Diagnostic only, not consumed by the chain. It reports Spearman rho between Katz-Bonacich centrality on build_P and the optimizer allocation, money and score. It reads low rho as the allocator pricing stance, receptivity and leverage beyond centrality.
bearings.transfer_conditions: An allocation-centrality correlation, high or low, can come from where the opponent places money rather than from a preference for centrality. Any reading of rho should be stratified by industry-money placement, or labelled UNSTRATIFIED. Rho here is a heuristic diagnostic, not evidence of influence. The paper's evidence comes from one email network.

bearings.paper_claim: In the discrete regime (K nodes at fixed gain), optima are driven mainly by degree (hub targeting). Shadowing and shielding matter mostly in the continuous regime, and shielding weakens as the opponent spreads (K = 256).
bearings.system_side: The frontier and coalition engines pick discrete A seeds under a progressive two-colour first-to-reach IC race against fixed anti seeds, with bystanders turned by industry money. Lazy greedy runs up to 60 seeds with CRN draws.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The dynamics differ: IC is progressive (an activated node stays activated), while the voter model is reversible. Only the regime point carries over: seed-set optimisers will tend toward hubs, and opponent-aware placement matters more when allocation is continuous. Weak evidence; one network, no noise.

gaps_exposed: Money does not propagate in the flip model or the joint optimizer: CU dollars change only the funded member's pflip (optimize.py:64-72). The paper's main mechanism, shielding the neighbours of opponent-targeted nodes, therefore cannot appear in any allocation the system produces.

Opponent allocation is fixed (ind = fm.ind0 at optimize.py:59), so the allocator best-responds to a frozen opponent. The system has no test of how its plan fares if industry PACs re-optimise; the paper's two-active-controller result says that equilibrium is uniform allocation.

An opponent-share field w_b (build_opposition_prior.py:1425-1440) is labelled for a 'shadowing layer', and contested_bills.py ships a counterparty registry, but no engine consumes either (contested_bills.py:9 says 'no consumer exists today').

The paper says the direction of the best response depends on budget ratio Ba/Bb. The system never computes per-bill or per-topic CU vs counterparty budget ratios, so it cannot tell whether shadowing or avoidance would apply.

The paper's exploitability result (Eq 6) says a non-uniform opponent is most exploitable on low-degree nodes. The system has no diagnostic of where industry money departs from uniform relative to network degree.
flags: Citation scope: contested_bills (Paul's position list) cites 'Romero Moreno 2021' for a counterparty term. The paper is an abstract, unnoised voter model on one 1,133-node academic email network, with no lobbying, election or legislative data. It supports the concept of an opponent-aware allocation, not any parameter or effect size.

D-025 wording: the paper's 'influence' and 'vote share' are steady-state model outputs. Any shadowing or shielding score built from it must be described as a heuristic model output, not closeness, access or the probability of a vote.
D-021: an opponent allocation w_b for shadowing must come from FEC money (as build_opposition_prior.py's basis does), never from LDA spend used as a weight.
DE-062: the claim that emergent shadowing would follow from the b term of a/(a+b) in the optimizer is this agent's inference. It is UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it.
The paper's internal inconsistency (|Z| = 9 at line 302 vs 7 at line 307) and its reliance on an unread S1 Appendix for other topologies limit how far its generality claims can be relied on.
No conflict with the rejected SNA proposals: the paper argues neither for dropping regular cosponsorship edges nor for per-edge volume normalisation.
rel.paul_alignment: This agrees with Paul's stated takeaway on contested bills: explicit inter-industry conflict over a bill is 'vital for political intelligence', and he wants rival industries modelled (Kim J. 2025 margin note). The paper gives that wish a formal shape: the response to a rival should depend on where the rival spends and on the budget ratio. It goes beyond his reading in two ways. First, the right response can be to avoid the rival's targets when CU is outspent. Second, a frozen-opponent plan is exploitable once the rival also optimises. His positions on the joint optimizer (adaptive greedy plus CELF, a learned policy later) do not mention opponent placement. They are therefore stale relative to what the system already holds: an unconsumed w_b 'shadowing layer' and an unwired registry. Neither the notes nor the system have taken up the paper's main mechanism, shielding, which the system's node-local money term cannot express.

related.why: Competitive influence maximisation in voter dynamics, adding timing and network heterogeneity, which addresses this paper's time-invariant-strategy limitation.
Competitive IC is the model behind the system's two-colour cascade race. This paper gives the voter-model (reversible) counterpart with an opponent-aware best response.
Competitive threshold models, which the flip model cites for having no submodularity guarantee. This paper instead proves concavity and a unique equilibrium in the continuous voter model.

Both derive equilibrium allocations across a network. B-P predict money loads on Katz-Bonacich centrality; this paper shows that a centrality correlation can be a by-product of the opponent's placement, which affects how kb_benchmark is read.
Both test whether simple heuristics approach optimised allocations; here shadowing and shielding outperform degree heuristics in the continuous regime.
Per-bill support and oppose positions by industry are the observed opponent placement that a shadowing response on contested bills would need.
